title: MATH2010 Module 12: Inner Product, Length, and Orthogonality

questions.q: Compute u • v for u = (3, −1, 4, 2) and v = (2, 5, −1, 3) (column vectors in R⁴).
questions.explain: Multiply matching entries and add: 3·2 + (−1)·5 + 4·(−1) + 2·3 = 6 − 5 − 4 + 6 = 3. The dot product is a scalar.

questions.q: Treating vectors in Rⁿ as n×1 matrices, which matrix product equals u • v?
questions.explain: u • v = uᵀv: a 1×n row times an n×1 column is 1×1, the number u₁v₁ + … + uₙvₙ. Both uvᵀ and vuᵀ are n×n matrices, and uᵀvᵀ (1×n times 1×n) is not defined.

questions.q: Which statements hold for all u, v, w in Rⁿ and every scalar c?
choices: (u + v) • w = u • w + v • w
v • v > 0 for every v in Rⁿ
u • v = 0 only if u = 0 or v = 0
questions.explain: The first three are the symmetry, distributive, and scalar properties. (cu) • (cv) = c²(u • v), since c comes out once from each side. v • v ≥ 0, with equality for v = 0, so '> 0 for every v' fails. Nonzero vectors can have dot product 0, for example (1, 0) • (0, 1) = 0.

questions.q: Suppose u • u = 4, u • v = −3, and v • v = 10. Compute (u + v) • (u + v).
Suppose u • u = 4, u • v = −3, and v • v = 10. Compute (2u − v) • (u + 3v).
questions.explain: Expand like an ordinary product: 2(u • u) + 6(u • v) − (v • u) − 3(v • v) = 8 − 18 + 3 − 30 = −37. Symmetry lets you replace v • u with u • v = −3.

questions.q: If v • v = 0, then v must be the zero vector.
questions.explain: v • v = v₁² + v₂² + … + vₙ² is a sum of squares, which is 0 only when every entry is 0. This is property 5 of the inner product.

questions.q: Which is the unit vector in the direction of x = (0, 3, −1, 4, −5)?
questions.explain: ‖x‖² = 0 + 9 + 1 + 16 + 25 = 51, so ‖x‖ = √51, and you divide x by √51. Dividing by 51 forgets the square root. 13 comes from adding the absolute values of the entries instead of their squares. The last choice has length 1 but points the opposite way.

questions.q: If ‖v‖ = 4, what is ‖−3v‖?
questions.explain: ‖cv‖ = |c|‖v‖, so ‖−3v‖ = |−3|·4 = 12. Lengths are never negative.

questions.q: Find the scalar c > 0 that makes c(2, −1, 2) a unit vector. Enter a decimal.
questions.explain: ‖(2, −1, 2)‖ = √(4 + 1 + 4) = 3, so c = 1/‖v‖ = 1/3 ≈ 0.3333. Since c > 0, the direction does not change.

questions.q: Find dist(x, y) for x = (3, 0, 1, 5) and y = (1, 1, −1, 1).
questions.explain: dist(x, y) = ‖x − y‖. x − y = (2, −1, 2, 4), and ‖x − y‖² = 4 + 1 + 4 + 16 = 25, so the distance is 5.

questions.q: Let x = (1, −2, 3, −1) and y = (−1, 2, −3, 1). What is dist(x, y)?
questions.explain: x − y = (2, −4, 6, −2), so ‖x − y‖² = 4 + 16 + 36 + 4 = 60 and dist(x, y) = √60 = 2√15. The answer 0 comes from ‖x‖ − ‖y‖ (both lengths are √15), which is not the distance. Here y = −x points the opposite way. 60 forgets the square root.

questions.q: For all u, v in Rⁿ, ‖u + v‖ = ‖u‖ + ‖v‖.
questions.explain: Only the triangle inequality ‖u + v‖ ≤ ‖u‖ + ‖v‖ holds in general. Counterexample: u = (1, 0), v = (−1, 0) gives ‖u + v‖ = 0 but ‖u‖ + ‖v‖ = 2.

questions.q: Which equation is the definition of u and v in Rⁿ being orthogonal (perpendicular)?
questions.explain: u + v and u − v are the two diagonals of the parallelogram on u and v. The diagonals are equal exactly when the parallelogram is a rectangle, so u and v meet at a right angle. A theorem then turns this into the working test u • v = 0.

questions.q: Using the dot-product properties, ‖u + v‖² − ‖u − v‖² simplifies to:
questions.explain: (‖u‖² + 2u • v + ‖v‖²) − (‖u‖² − 2u • v + ‖v‖²) = 4(u • v). So ‖u + v‖ = ‖u − v‖ exactly when u • v = 0, which is why orthogonal ⇔ u • v = 0. 2‖u‖² + 2‖v‖² is the sum of the two squares, not the difference.

questions.q: Which pairs of vectors are orthogonal?
questions.explain: Check each dot product: −20 − 15 + 35 = 0 (orthogonal); 4 + 2 − 4 = 2 (not); 2 − 2 + 0 + 0 = 0 (orthogonal); 3 + 3 = 6 (not). The zero vector is orthogonal to every vector, since 0 • v = 0.

questions.q: Find k so that (k, 2, −1) is orthogonal to (3, −4, 1).
questions.explain: Set the dot product to 0: 3k − 8 − 1 = 0, so 3k = 9 and k = 3.

questions.q: u and v are orthogonal, with ‖u‖ = 5 and ‖v‖ = 12. Find ‖u − v‖.
questions.explain: ‖u − v‖² = ‖u‖² − 2(u • v) + ‖v‖² = 25 − 0 + 144 = 169, so ‖u − v‖ = 13. By the definition of orthogonality this also equals ‖u + v‖.

questions.q: Let x = (2, −3, 5) and y = (−10, 5, 7). Compute ‖x + y‖².
questions.explain: x + y = (−8, 2, 12), so ‖x + y‖² = 64 + 4 + 144 = 212. This equals ‖x‖² + ‖y‖² = 38 + 174, which is the Pythagorean theorem. It holds because x • y = −20 − 15 + 35 = 0.

questions.q: If ‖u + v‖² = ‖u‖² + ‖v‖², then u and v must be orthogonal.
questions.explain: ‖u + v‖² = ‖u‖² + 2(u • v) + ‖v‖², so the equation forces 2(u • v) = 0. The Pythagorean relation works in both directions.

questions.q: For any matrix A, (Row A)⊥ equals:
questions.explain: Entry i of Ax is (row i of A) • x, so Ax = 0 means x is orthogonal to every row, and therefore to all of Row A. So (Row A)⊥ = Nul A.

questions.q: For any matrix A, (Col A)⊥ equals:
questions.explain: The columns of A are the rows of Aᵀ, so Col A = Row Aᵀ and (Col A)⊥ = (Row Aᵀ)⊥ = Nul Aᵀ. Writing Nul A here is a common mistake.

questions.q: Let A be the 2×2 matrix with rows (1, −2) and (−1, 2). What is (Row A)⊥?
questions.explain: (Row A)⊥ = Nul A. A row reduces to rows (1, −2), (0, 0), so x₁ = 2x₂ and x = x₂(2, 1). Check: (2, 1) • (1, −2) = 0. Span{(1, −2)} is Row A itself.

questions.q: Let A be the 2×2 matrix with rows (1, −2) and (−1, 2). What is (Col A)⊥?
questions.explain: (Col A)⊥ = Nul Aᵀ. Aᵀ has rows (1, −1), (−2, 2), which reduce to x₁ = x₂, so the answer is Span{(1, 1)}. Check: Col A = Span{(1, −1)} and (1, 1) • (1, −1) = 0. Span{(2, 1)} is (Row A)⊥.

questions.q: Let W = Span{(1, 0, 2), (0, 1, −1)} in R³. Which vectors are in W⊥?
questions.explain: W⊥ is the null space of the matrix with rows (1, 0, 2), (0, 1, −1): x₁ = −2x₃, x₂ = x₃, so W⊥ = Span{(−2, 1, 1)}. (4, −2, −2) is a multiple of it, and 0 is in every subspace. (2, 1, 1) • (1, 0, 2) = 4 and (1, 1, 1) • (1, 0, 2) = 3, so those two are not in W⊥.

questions.q: A is a 5×7 matrix of rank 3. What is the dimension of (Row A)⊥?
questions.explain: (Row A)⊥ = Nul A, a subspace of R⁷. By the Rank Theorem, dim Nul A = 7 − 3 = 4. This matches dim Row A + dim (Row A)⊥ = 3 + 4 = 7.

questions.q: A is a 5×7 matrix of rank 3. (Col A)⊥ is a subspace of which space, and what is its dimension?
questions.explain: The columns of A have 5 entries, so Col A and (Col A)⊥ = Nul Aᵀ are in R⁵. Aᵀ is 7×5 with rank 3, so dim Nul Aᵀ = 5 − 3 = 2. Check: 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.q: If W = Span{w₁, …, wₖ}, then to show v is in W⊥ it is enough to check that v • wᵢ = 0 for each spanning vector wᵢ.
questions.explain: Any u in W is c₁w₁ + … + cₖwₖ, so v • u = c₁(v • w₁) + … + cₖ(v • wₖ) = 0. This is why W⊥ is the null space of the matrix whose rows are the spanning vectors.

questions.q: To show that a set of 4 nonzero vectors is orthogonal, how many dot products must you check?
questions.explain: Every pair must have dot product 0. With r vectors there are r(r − 1)/2 pairs: 4·3/2 = 6. Order doesn't matter because u • v = v • u, so 12 double-counts.

questions.q: Every linearly independent set in Rⁿ is orthogonal.
questions.explain: The theorem only goes one way: orthogonal sets are independent. (1, 0) and (1, 1) are independent, but their dot product is 1.

questions.q: {(1, 2), (0, 0)} is an orthogonal set.
questions.explain: The dot product is 0, but the definition of an orthogonal set requires every vector to be nonzero. A set containing 0 is also linearly dependent, so allowing it would break the theorem that orthogonal sets are independent.

questions.q: Let x = (1, −2, 3, 7), y = (−1, 2, −3, 2), z = (5, 4, 1, 0). Which statement about {x, y, z} is correct?
choices: Orthogonal; a basis for the 3-dimensional subspace it spans, not R⁴
Orthogonal; three orthogonal vectors are enough for a basis of R⁴
Not orthogonal, because x • y ≠ 0, so the set is dependent
Orthogonal, but linearly dependent since R⁴ needs four vectors
questions.explain: x • y = −1 − 4 − 9 + 14 = 0, x • z = 5 − 8 + 3 + 0 = 0, and y • z = −5 + 8 − 3 + 0 = 0, and all three vectors are nonzero, so the set is orthogonal and therefore independent. Three vectors cannot span R⁴, so it is an orthogonal basis only for the subspace it spans.

questions.q: To prove an orthogonal set {v₁, …, vᵣ} is linearly independent, start from c₁v₁ + … + cᵣvᵣ = 0 and dot both sides with vⱼ. What equation is left?
questions.explain: Every cross term vᵢ • vⱼ (i ≠ j) is 0, leaving cⱼ(vⱼ • vⱼ) = 0. Since vⱼ ≠ 0, vⱼ • vⱼ > 0, so cⱼ = 0. This holds for every j.

questions.q: {v₁, v₂, v₃} = {(1, 1, 0), (1, −1, 1), (−1, 1, 2)} is an orthogonal basis of R³. Write y = (4, −2, 1) as c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + c₃v₃. What is c₂? Enter a decimal.
u₁ = (1, 1, 1), u₂ = (−7, 2, 5), u₃ = (3, −12, 9) form an orthogonal basis of R³. Which expresses x = (−2, 1, 4) in this basis?
questions.explain: cᵢ = (x • uᵢ)/(uᵢ • uᵢ): c₁ = 3/3 = 1, c₂ = 36/78 = 6/13, c₃ = 18/234 = 1/13. The other choices use only the numerators, divide by ‖uᵢ‖ instead of ‖uᵢ‖², or flip the fractions.

questions.q: If {v₁, …, vᵣ} is an orthogonal basis for W and y is in W, the weight cᵢ in y = c₁v₁ + … + cᵣvᵣ is (y • vᵢ)/‖vᵢ‖.
questions.explain: The denominator is vᵢ • vᵢ = ‖vᵢ‖², not ‖vᵢ‖. Dotting y = Σ cₖvₖ with vᵢ kills every other term and leaves y • vᵢ = cᵢ(vᵢ • vᵢ).

questions.q: Find the orthogonal projection of y = (4, 7) onto W = Span{(2, 1)}.
questions.explain: proj_W y = ((y • v)/(v • v))v = (15/5)(2, 1) = (6, 3). (30, 15) forgets to divide by v • v, (6√5, 3√5) divides by ‖v‖ instead of ‖v‖², and (−2, 4) is the leftover piece z = y − ŷ.

questions.q: Write y = (4, 7) as ŷ + z, where ŷ is in Span{(2, 1)} and z is orthogonal to (2, 1). What is z?
questions.explain: ŷ = (15/5)(2, 1) = (6, 3), so z = y − ŷ = (−2, 4). Check: (−2, 4) • (2, 1) = 0. (−1, 2) is also orthogonal to (2, 1), but ŷ + z must equal y, and the decomposition is unique.

The basis is orthogonal: 1 − 1 + 0 = 0. Then y • v₁ / v₁ • v₁ = 6/2 = 3 and y • v₂ / v₂ • v₂ = 12/6 = 2, so ŷ = 3(1, 1, 0) + 2(1, −1, 2) = (5, 1, 4). (−1, 1, 1) is z = y − ŷ, (18, −6, 24) uses only the numerators, and (3, 2, 0) lists the weights rather than the vector.

questions.q: If y is orthogonal to every vector in the subspace W, then proj_W y equals:
questions.explain: y is in W⊥, so every numerator y • vᵢ in the projection formula is 0. In the decomposition y = ŷ + z, all of y is the z part.

questions.q: If y is already in the subspace W, then proj_W y = y.
questions.explain: With an orthogonal basis, the projection formula is the same as the weights formula, which rebuilds y exactly when y is in W. The orthogonal piece z is 0.

questions.q: If {v₁, v₂} is any basis of W (not necessarily orthogonal), then proj_W y = ((y • v₁)/(v₁ • v₁))v₁ + ((y • v₂)/(v₂ • v₂))v₂.
questions.explain: The formula needs an orthogonal basis. Example: W = R² with v₁ = (1, 0), v₂ = (1, 1), y = (0, 1). The projection should be y itself, but the formula gives 0·(1, 0) + (1/2)(1, 1) = (1/2, 1/2).

questions.q: Each y in Rⁿ can be written in only one way as ŷ + z with ŷ in W and z in W⊥, so two different orthogonal bases of W give the same ŷ.
questions.explain: The Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem says Rⁿ = W ⊕ W⊥ and the decomposition is unique, with ŷ = proj_W y and z = y − ŷ. The answer depends only on W, not on the basis you use for it.

questions.q: Replacing v with 5v changes the orthogonal projection of y onto Span{v}.
questions.explain: ((y • 5v)/(5v • 5v))(5v) = (5·5/25)((y • v)/(v • v))v, so the 5s cancel. The projection depends only on the line, not on which vector you choose on it.

questions.q: After computing ŷ = proj_W y and z = y − ŷ from an orthogonal basis {v₁, …, vᵣ} of W, which check catches arithmetic errors?
choices: z • vᵢ = 0 for each basis vector vᵢ
ŷ • vᵢ = 0 for each basis vector vᵢ
questions.explain: z must lie in W⊥, so it has to be orthogonal to every basis vector of W. ŷ lies in W, so ŷ • vᵢ is usually not 0, and nothing forces ‖z‖ = ‖ŷ‖. ŷ • z is actually 0.

questions.q: By the definition in 12.2, an m×n matrix U is called orthogonal when:
choices: its columns form an orthonormal set
its columns form an orthogonal set
it is square and det U = 1
all its entries lie between −1 and 1
questions.explain: U = [u₁ … uₙ] is orthogonal when {u₁, …, uₙ} is orthonormal: pairwise orthogonal and each of length 1. Orthogonal columns alone are not enough. (Many textbooks reserve the name for square matrices; this definition allows any m×n.)

questions.q: U is a 5×3 matrix with orthonormal columns. Which is always true?
questions.explain: Entry (i, j) of UᵀU is uᵢ • uⱼ, which is 1 on the diagonal and 0 off it, so UᵀU is the 3×3 identity. UUᵀ is 5×5 and is the projection onto Col U, not I₅. U is not square, so it has no inverse.

questions.q: U is an m×n orthogonal matrix and x, y are in Rⁿ. Which statements always hold?
choices: UUᵀw = w for every w in Rᵐ
questions.explain: (Ux) • (Uy) = xᵀUᵀUy = xᵀy = x • y, so dot products, lengths, and right angles are all preserved. UUᵀw is the projection of w onto Col U, which equals w only for w in Col U unless U is square. Ux is in Rᵐ and generally is not x.

questions.q: U is a 6×4 orthogonal matrix and x is a vector in R⁴ with ‖x‖ = 3. What is ‖U(2x)‖?
questions.explain: Orthogonal matrices preserve length, so ‖U(2x)‖ = ‖2x‖ = 2·3 = 6.

questions.q: Which matrices are orthogonal (columns orthonormal)?
questions.explain: (0, 1), (1, 0): unit length and orthogonal. (1, 1), (1, −1): orthogonal, but each has length √2. (3/5, 4/5), (4/5, −3/5): lengths √(9/25 + 16/25) = 1 and dot product 12/25 − 12/25 = 0. The 3×2 matrix also qualifies, since the definition allows non-square U. (2, 0), (0, 1/2): orthogonal, but the lengths are 2 and 1/2.

questions.q: If U is a square orthogonal matrix, then U⁻¹ equals:
questions.explain: UᵀU = I, and for a square matrix a one-sided inverse is the inverse, so U⁻¹ = Uᵀ. Inverting is just transposing. UᵀU is I itself.

questions.q: The formula proj_W y = UUᵀy, with U = [u₁ … uᵣ], holds when the columns of U are:
questions.explain: Uᵀy lists the numbers y • uᵢ, and multiplying by U gives (y • u₁)u₁ + … + (y • uᵣ)uᵣ. That is the projection only when each uᵢ • uᵢ = 1, so the basis must be orthonormal. With only an orthogonal basis, normalize first.

questions.q: u₁ = (1/3)(1, 2, 2) and u₂ = (1/3)(2, 1, −2) form an orthonormal basis of W, and U = [u₁ u₂]. For y = (3, 0, 0), what is UUᵀy?
questions.explain: Uᵀy = (u₁ • y, u₂ • y) = (1, 2). Then U(1, 2) = u₁ + 2u₂ = (1/3)(1 + 4, 2 + 2, 2 − 4) = (1/3)(5, 4, −2). (3, 0, 0) would be right only if y were in W.

questions.q: u₁ = (3/5, 4/5) and u₂ = (−4/5, 3/5) form an orthonormal basis of R². If y = (5, 10) = c₁u₁ + c₂u₂, what is c₁?
questions.explain: With an orthonormal basis, uᵢ • uᵢ = 1, so cᵢ = y • uᵢ. Then c₁ = 5(3/5) + 10(4/5) = 3 + 8 = 11 and c₂ = −4 + 6 = 2. Check: 11(3/5, 4/5) + 2(−4/5, 3/5) = (5, 10).

questions.q: Dividing each vector of an orthogonal basis of W by its length gives an orthonormal basis of W.
questions.explain: Scaling by a nonzero number keeps every pairwise dot product 0 and doesn't change the span, and each uᵢ = vᵢ/‖vᵢ‖ has length 1.
